title: Messaging framing cheat sheet: engineering functions
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a rapid, conversation-first cheat sheet for GTM and AE reps to frame Redwood Inference for three adjacent engineering audiences: ML engineers, backend engineers, and platform teams. The goal: give short, testable talk tracks, priority pain points, competitive differentiators tailored to day-to-day workflows, and a simple experiment plan for validating messages in outreach and demos.

High-level positioning anchor (one-liner):
Redwood Inference: production-grade inference that lets engineering teams deliver consistent latency and predictable costs across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments — without building and operating the inference stack.

Why separate messaging matters
- ML engineers focus on model fidelity, evals, and iteration velocity (inference as a research-to-prod bridge).
- Backend engineers care about latency, reliability, and integration surface (inference as a production service).
- Platform teams prioritize standardization, governance, and cost predictability (inference as an internal product).
Tailoring the framing increases relevance and shortens cycles from POC -> committed capacity.

Persona slices: pain, top-message, demo hooks, quick objections
1) ML engineers
- Top pain points: slow iteration loops when model changes require infra reprovisioning; opaque performance regressions after quantization; difficulty reproducing production token costs and latency.
- Top message: "Ship model improvements without rebuilding serving — Redwood preserves model fidelity while exposing per-prompt performance profiles so you can iterate faster."
- Demo hooks: show A/B rollout of model variants with per-prompt quality metrics + quick rollback; run a quantization suggestion that keeps eval scores within tolerance and halves token cost.
- Evidence bullets: recent internal evals show <1.5% quality delta after our quantization recommendations on Llama-variant workloads; integrated eval sets in console with anchored baselines.
- Likely objection & reply: "We manage our own endpoints already." -> "Totally — Redwood plugs into your CI and exports the same metrics; most teams keep model dev in-place and use Redwood to standardize serving and rollback safety."

2) Backend engineers
- Top pain points: unpredictable tail latency, integration surface area with auth/observability, retry and fallback complexity, and cost spikes under burst.
- Top message: "Treat inference like any other API service: consistent SLA, transparent cost/latency breakdowns, and built-in fallbacks to avoid production outages."
- Demo hooks: show token-level latency breakdown, a live canary switch over to cheaper model variant under high load, and how a routing policy fails over to a different region with no code change.
- Evidence bullets: console shows per-route latency P95/P99, token-cost waterfall, and routing policy examples used by customers to avoid outages.
- Likely objection & reply: "We can't depend on turnkey routes for sensitive infra." -> "Redwood Dedicated and Private let you isolate traffic; routing rules are configurable and audited — you keep control."

3) Platform teams
- Top pain points: lack of centralized policies for model versioning, compliance with audit/KMS requirements, and inability to enforce cost controls across product teams.
- Top message: "Give teams a single, policy-driven inference platform with observability and enforceable cost/variance guardrails."
- Demo hooks: policy templates (model pinning, allowed quantization levels), per-team cost quotas and alerts, and audit log flows to external SIEM/KMS.
- Evidence bullets: sample policy JSON, successful private deployments with KMS integration, and billing granularity down to token+route.
- Likely objection & reply: "We already have internal infra for governance." -> "Redwood is designed to sit behind your control plane (VPC/private), and provides policy primitives that integrate with existing SSO/KMS and your infra-as-code."

Competitive contrast (how to talk about competitors in one sentence)
- Cloud-managed model hosts (big cloud vendors): "They give compute and endpoints but leave you to solve batching, caching, and routing policies; Redwood ships those production-first levers with actionable recommendations."
- LLM API incumbents (simple APIs): "Quick to use but opaque on unit economics and limited for private deployments — Redwood gives both an easy API and enterprise-grade hosting/privates."
- Inference runtimes/self-hosted solutions: "High control but high ops burden; Redwood combines a curated runtime with orchestration and policy tooling so teams don’t rebuild the same ops work."

Key proof points and numbers to use (short bullets)
- Typical P95 latency reduction: 20–40% after tuning batching + KV prefix caching.
- Cost delta: customers see 25–60% token-cost reduction when adopting recommended batching + quantization profiles for high-volume workloads.
- Rollouts: canary -> 100% migration in under an hour for standard setups with built-in rollback.

Short outreach talk tracks (cold email / SDR)
- ML engineer (subject): "Ship model updates faster without the serve rewrite"
  Body (one-liner): "Hi X — teams we work with cut time-to-production for model updates from weeks to days by decoupling model dev from serving operations. Quick question: do you currently pin model versions in prod or rebuild infra every time you change quantization?"
- Backend engineer (subject): "Make inference a first-class API in your stack"
  Body (one-liner): "Hi X — curious if you get unexpected latency/cold-starts from LLM endpoints during traffic spikes. We provide per-route SLOs and automated fallbacks so product code doesn't have to handle degraded inference modes."
- Platform lead (subject): "Standardize inference across orgs with policy & cost controls"
  Body (one-liner): "Hi X — would you be open to a 20-minute walkthrough of a policy-driven model rollout that enforces cost and quantization constraints across teams?"

Demo flow template (7–10 minutes)
1) 60s: customer context and shared pain (mirror what they said).
2) 90s: show console: per-route latency + token-cost waterfall.
3) 2–3 min: live policy change: pin model/rollback + canary -> demonstrate telemetry and rollback.
4) 2 min: show optimization suggestion (batching or quantization) and expected cost/quality delta on their baseline.
5) 30–60s: next steps and ask for a short POC (volume sample: 1–2M tokens/day or integration with existing dev flow).

Message experiments and metrics to validate
- Channel A/B: ML-engineer focused subject line vs generic platform line; measure reply rate and meeting rate.
- Demo variant: show quantization-first vs failover-first; track which slides lead to engagement and PO C conversions.
- Validation metrics: reply rate, qualified meeting rate, POC conversion within 60 days, and time-to-first-successful-rollback in POC.

Risks & weak signals to watch
- Copy that over-promises quality-preservation after quantization — monitor post-demo follow-ups for technical pushback.
- Backend engineers may ask for infra diagrams; include a one-slide infra mapping to reduce friction.
- Platform teams will ask about audit trails and KMS — ensure engineering oncall can answer integration specifics in follow-ups.

Suggested collateral to pair with outreach
- 1-page "Quick technical checklist" for ML teams: CI hooks, eval sets, model pinning steps.
- 2-slide infra map for backend: network flow, auth, and failover examples.
- 1-page policy template pack for platform: sample rules and quota examples.

Next steps (owner: Sofia Martinez)
- Run A/B cold email test this quarter (two variants) and report reply/meeting conversion after 4 weeks.
- Build the 2-slide infra map and one-pager policy pack (collab: Priya + Liam).
- Collect three POC case studies to turn into short evidence bullets for sales.

Notes to self (scratchpad):
- Keep the demo <10m for discovery calls.
- Pull one customer example where Redwood avoided a production outage via routing fallback.
- Keep bench numbers ready but hedge language: "typical" or "customer-observed" to avoid overclaiming.
